title: Holi: the festival of colors
hook: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali and King Bali, who kept his word and comes home once a year. Your line was light the way home. Did you keep an inconvenient promise? Day six hundred eighty-eight.

At the Holi bonfire, Prahlad walks out of the fire. But the story doesn't stop there, and the Bhagavata Purana carries it further. His father, the king Hiranyakashipu, has tried everything to kill him, and nothing works. Finally, in a rage, he stands in front of his son in the great hall and asks: this Vishnu of yours, who you say is everywhere. Is he in this pillar? The boy says yes. And the king strikes the pillar.
screen: `THE FIRE WAS NOT THE END.` → `IS HE IN THIS PILLAR?` → `THE KING STRIKES IT.`

segments.voice: To understand what happens next, you need the king's boon. Long before, after fierce austerities, Hiranyakashipu had been granted protection, as the Bhagavata tells it, with a long list of conditions. No man or animal could kill him. Not by day or by night. Not inside or outside. Not on the earth or in the sky. Not with any weapon. He thought he'd closed every door. When he strikes the pillar, it splits open, and out comes Narasimha: Vishnu as half man, half lion. Neither man nor animal. He seizes the king at twilight, neither day nor night. On the threshold of the hall, neither inside nor outside. Lays him across his lap, neither earth nor sky. And ends him with his claws, which are not a weapon. Every door the king thought he had closed, opened. Then Narasimha is so terrible in his fury that even the gods are afraid to come near. They send the boy. Prahlad walks up and bows, and Narasimha calms and puts his hand on his head. And when Narasimha offers him any blessing he wants, Prahlad asks for something astonishing: that his father, who tried to kill him again and again, be purified and freed. The Bhagavata says the wish is granted. That's where Prahlad's story ends, and some readers hear in it a key to the morning of colors. The boy who survived everything doesn't ask for revenge. He asks for his father's release. In some villages, people roast ears of the new wheat or barley in the Holi bonfire and share them. A meal of fresh grain, cooked in the fire that ended the cruelty, and eaten together.
screen: `NOT MAN OR BEAST, NOT DAY OR NIGHT.` · `NARASIMHA BURSTS FROM THE PILLAR.` · `ONLY THE BOY CAN CALM HIM.` · `PRAHLAD ASKS FOR HIS FATHER'S RELEASE.` · then, large: `NOT REVENGE, BUT RELEASE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring back the small grudge you set on the fire a couple of weeks ago, or a new one. This time, try what Prahlad did, just a little. Not forgiving everything. Just wishing the other person well, once, for one breath: may they be free of whatever made them act that way. Then let it go with the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Holi. The fire for Prahlad, Narasimha from the pillar, and a boy who asked not for revenge but for his father's release.
Your line: everyone's the same color today. Today, wish one person well who once wished you ill, even just in your head. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: At Holika Dahan, some communities roast ears of new wheat or barley in the bonfire and share them; the next morning, Holi is often a day for visiting, reconciling and starting fresh with neighbors and relatives.

original.note: Sanskrit nara (man) + siṃha (lion): Vishnu as the man-lion.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Holi story ends when Prahlad walks out of the fire.
what it means: it goes on to Narasimha, and to Prahlad asking for his father's release.
what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata's seventh book gives the boon's conditions (7.3), Narasimha's appearance (7.8) and Prahlad's request for his father (7.10).
